title: Ten pounds (Luke 19:11–27)
hookLine: Luke's version of the talents: be faithful with a little

lines: WHAT TO DO IN THE MEANTIME.
cards: Jesus is now nigh to Jerusalem, and Luke tells us what's in the air: "they thought that the kingdom of God should immediately appear." Any day now.
A healer and teacher heading into the capital with a crowd behind him, and people ready for a coronation.
So he tells them about a coronation that takes a long time to arrive, and what to do in the meantime with very little in your hands.

teach.b: A nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom and return.

Some scholars think listeners would have recognized that: the historian Josephus tells how, after Herod the Great died, his son Archelaus traveled to Rome to have his rule confirmed, and a delegation went after him to protest.
In the story, too, the citizens send word: "We will not have this man to reign over us."

teach.h: ONE POUND EACH, ALL THE SAME.
teach.b: Before he leaves, he gives each of ten servants one pound. In Greek, a mina: a real sum, but small next to a kingdom. And here's the big difference from Matthew's parable of the talents.
There, servants get different amounts. Here, everyone gets exactly the same.
His instruction, in the King James Bible: "Occupy till I come." Occupy means do business, put it to work. When he returns, the first servant says: "Lord, thy pound hath gained ten pounds."
And: "Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities." A very little. Ten cities.
The reward is wildly out of proportion to the test. Another made five.
Then one says: "Lord, behold, here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin." Safe and useless, because he was afraid.
The traditional reading hears the nobleman as Christ, gone away and coming back, asking what his people did with what they were given.
Some modern readers notice how harsh the nobleman is and hear a warning about earthly kings instead.
Either way, the question is ours: what do you do with a very little, while you wait?

how: In Christian teaching, gifts and talents are often described as given by God to be used for others, and churches encourage people to discover and use their gifts in service, in the congregation and beyond.

games.q: you're a servant handed one pound by a nobleman who's leaving to receive a kingdom. you're afraid of him. what do you do?
o: trade with it and see what happens.
wrap it in a napkin and keep it safe.
spend it before he gets back.
games.why: one servant says: "here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin" because he feared his master. safe, and unused.

practice: Think of one small thing you keep wrapped up: a skill you rarely use, a little spare time, a knack for listening, cooking or fixing things.
Notice what's kept it in the napkin, fear of getting it wrong or a sense it's too small to matter, and picture it put to work for someone else. If you pray, offer it back to God.
